```{python}
#| code-fold: show
lowest = error_rate == error_rate.min()
best_cutoffs = cutoffs[lowest]
# A new stretch of lowest error starts wherever `lowest` turns from False to True.
n_stretches = np.sum(np.diff(lowest.astype(int)) == 1) + int(lowest[0])
print(error_rate.min(), best_cutoffs.min(), best_cutoffs.max(), n_stretches)
```

No.
The curve in @fig-error-rate-curve is a staircase.
The [error rate](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/metrics.html#def-error-rate) changes only where $\param$ crosses one of the
`r length(unique(py$ink_01))` values that the center ink takes,
and it is flat everywhere in between,
so its slope is 0 wherever the slope exists.
Gradient descent would never move.

The grid of cutoffs in steps of 0.01 reaches the lowest error rate,
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(py$error_rate))`%
(`r round(sum(py$is_01) * min(py$error_rate))` of the `r sum(py$is_01)` images),
on `r py$n_stretches` separate stretches
between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(py$best_cutoffs))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(py$best_cutoffs))`,
and it found them by trying each cutoff in turn.
That works for one [parameter](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-parameter),
but a network has thousands of weights,
and trying every combination of their values is out of reach.

:::
